finalAnswer:
RIN 2060-AV16 is a completed rulemaking. EPA issued the final rule on March 8, 2024.

**What it is:** "Standards of Performance for New, Reconstructed, and Modified Sources and Emissions Guidelines for Existing Sources: Oil and Natural Gas Sector Climate Review." It's an EPA Office of Air and Radiation rule under Clean Air Act §111(b) and (d), codified at 40 CFR Part 60. It's also known as the NSPS OOOOb / EG OOOOc methane rule, and its docket is EPA-HQ-OAR-2021-0317.

**Timeline:**
- **Nov 15, 2021:** Proposed rule (86 FR 63110).
- **Dec 17, 2021:** Comment period extended to Jan 31, 2022 (86 FR 71603).
- **Dec 6, 2022:** Supplemental proposed rule (87 FR 74702).
- **Mar 8, 2024:** Final rule (89 FR 16820).
- **Aug 1, 2024:** Interim final rule with corrections and a request for comments (docket document 2024-13206).

**Unified Agenda:** The RIN appears in the Spring 2021 through Spring 2024 agendas. I didn't find it in later ones.

**Limits of what I found:**
- I couldn't retrieve a current status page for this RIN. The Spring 2025 Unified Agenda page I tried only listed the earlier agenda editions.
- I didn't search for anything after the August 2024 correction. EPA, Congress or the courts may have taken later actions on these standards, such as reconsideration, compliance-deadline changes or litigation. Those may sit under different RINs or dockets.
- To check for later actions, search the docket on regulations.gov or the RIN on federalregister.gov: https://www.federalregister.gov/regulations/2060-AV16

On November 15, 2021, the EPA proposed new source performance standards and emission guidelines for crude oil and natural gas facilities. (86 FR 63110). This action was in response to the January 20, 2021, Executive Order titled "Protecting Public Health and the Environment and Restoring Science to Tackle the Climate Crisis," which directs the EPA to take certain actions by September 2021 to reduce methane and volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions in the oil and natural gas sector. Specifically, the Executive order directs the EPA to review the new source performance standards (NSPS) issued in 2020 for the oil and gas sector and, as appropriate and consistent with applicable law, consider publishing for notice and comment a proposed rule suspending, revising, or rescinding that action. The Executive Order further directs the EPA to consider proposing new regulations to establish comprehensive emission guidelines for emissions from the exploration and production, transmission, processing, and storage segments. | | | **Agency:** Environmental Protection Agency(EPA) | **Priority:** Economically Significant | | **RIN Status:** Previously published in the Unified Agenda | **Agenda Stage of Rulemaking:** Proposed Rule Stage | | **Major:** Yes | **Unfunded Mandates:** No | | **CFR Citation:** [40 CFR 60](javascript:leavePage\('40 CFR 60', 2022, 'CFR'\))    subpart OOOOa     (To search for a specific CFR, visit the [Code of Federal Regulations.](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/reginfo/leaveregs.myjsp?toi=159)) | | | **Legal Authority:** [42 U.S.C. 7411](javascript:leavePage\('42 U.S.C. 7411', 2022, 'L'\)) | | **Legal Deadline:**  None **Statement of Need:** Executive Order 13990, “Protecting Public Health and the Environment and Restoring Science to Tackle the Climate Crisis”. The Executive order directs the EPA to consider proposing, by September 2021, a rulemaking to reduce methane emissions in the Oil and Natural Gas source category by suspending, revising, or rescinding previously issued new source performance standards. It also instructs the EPA to consider proposing new regulations to establish comprehensive standards of performance and emission guidelines for methane and volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions from existing operations in the oil and natural gas sector, including the exploration and production, processing, transmission and storage segments. **Summary of the Legal Basis:** Clean Air Act section 111(b) provides the legal framework for establishing greenhouse gas emission standards (in the form of limitations on methane) and volatile organic compounds for new oil and natural gas sources. finalAnswer:
**RIN 1904-AG06 has not been finalized as far as I could confirm, so it has no effective date yet.**

The RIN is DOE's "Energy Conservation Program: Test Procedures for Commercial Warm Air Furnaces." Here is what the Unified Agenda entry on reginfo.gov (the 2026 edition) shows:

- **Stage:** Final Rule Stage, meaning it is still pending.
- **Proposed rule:** DOE published the proposal on 05/16/2025 (90 FR 20909). The public meeting was 05/29/2025 and comments closed 07/15/2025.
- **Final action:** listed as "to be determined" with a target of **October 2026**. The entry gives no day.
- **What it does:** it would rescind Appendix B, the "Thermal Efficiency Two" test method. DOE tentatively found it unduly burdensome. Appendix A (Thermal Efficiency) would stay in force. DOE labels the rule deregulatory.
- **Legal deadline:** none.

**When it could take effect:** a final rule normally takes effect on a date set in the rule itself. That is often 30 to 60 days after Federal Register publication, but I can't give a date until it is published. If it came out in October 2026 as targeted, an effective date would likely fall in late 2026 or early 2027. That is only an estimate.

**Limits of this check:** my search of the Federal Register and DOE sites for a published final rule came back with nothing relevant. The agenda target date is also only a projection and often slips. Before relying on this, check the Federal Register or regulations.gov for the DOE docket on commercial warm air furnace test procedures, or reginfo.gov for the latest agenda entry.

The U.S. Department of Energy ("DOE" or "the Department") proposes to revise the Department's current rulemaking guidance titled "Procedures, Interpretations, and Policies for Consideration of New or Revised Energy Conservation Standards and Test Procedures for Consumer Products and Certain Commercial/Industrial Equipment" ("Process Rule"), which was last modified in 2020.  These proposed revisions, which are the first of two sets of revisions to the Process Rule that DOE intends to propose to make, are consistent with longstanding DOE practice prior to the 2020 amendment and would remove unnecessary obstacles to DOE's ability to meet its statutory obligations under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act ("EPCA") and other applicable law.  These proposed changes would include modifying the Process Rule to remove its mandatory application, removing its recently-added threshold for determining when significant energy savings is met, removing the current provision regarding the use of a comparative analysis when selecting potential energy conservation standards, and reverting to its prior guidance for determining whether a trial standard level is economically justified, among others. As part of its implementation of the Executive order, Unleashing American Energy (Jan. 20, 2025), the Department of Energy (DOE or the Department) is proposing to amend the test procedure for commercial warm air furnaces adopted under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act by rescinding Appendix B, Uniform Test Method for Measurement of the Energy Efficiency of Commercial Warm Air Furnaces (Thermal Efficiency Two). Upon further evaluation, the Department has tentatively determined that Appendix B is unduly burdensome to conduct, thereby failing to meet the statutory criteria for adoption of a test procedure. Commercial warm air furnaces will continue to be subject to the testing requirements of Appendix A, Uniform Test Method for Measurement of the Energy Efficiency of Commercial Warm Air Furnaces (Thermal Efficiency), which DOE has tentatively concluded meets the applicable statutory requirements. ![Public Education for Noncitizen Students: Understanding Plyler v. Doe](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/understanding_plyer_v_doe_feature.jpg)

In June 1982, the Supreme Court issued its decision in a case known as _Plyler v. Doe_, a landmark constitutional decision holding that states cannot deny K-12 students’ public education on account of their immigration status.[1](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/fact-sheet/plyler-v-doe-public-education-noncitizen-students/#fn1) By a 5-4 vote, the Court held that a Texas statute that withheld funds for the education of undocumented children violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court reasoned that any resources that might be saved by excluding undocumented children from public schools were far outweighed by the harms imposed on society at large from denying them an education.

For more than 40 years, _Plyler_ has ensured access to education for children regardless of immigration status, but recent legislation considered by several states continues to threaten that right. Since January 1, 2025, lawmakers in 8 states have introduced over 15 bills that challenge core aspects of _Plyler._[2](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/fact-sheet/plyler-v-doe-public-education-noncitizen-students/#fn2) This includes legislation requiring schools to collect immigration status information at enrollment, requiring undocumented students to pay tuition, or prohibiting the enrollment of undocumented students altogether. Five Federal Register documents are filed under docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2021-0317, the EPA's "Oil and Natural Gas Sector Climate Review" (the methane rule, Subparts OOOOb and OOOOc). I took the list from the Federal Register API's docket filter.

## Documents in the docket

| Date | Type | Document | Citation | Doc. No. |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021-11-15 | Proposed Rule | Original proposal | 86 FR 63110 | 2021-24202 |
| 2021-12-17 | Proposed Rule | Extension of comment period | 86 FR 71603 | 2021-27312 |
| 2022-12-06 | Proposed Rule | Supplemental proposal | 87 FR 74702 | 2022-24675 |
| 2024-03-08 | Rule | **Final rule** | 89 FR 16820 | 2024-00366 |
| 2024-08-01 | Rule | Correction to the final rule | 89 FR 62872 | 2024-13206 |

Each document's page is at `https://www.federalregister.gov/d/<document number>`.

## Where it stands

The rulemaking in this docket is finished. The EPA finalized the rule on March 8, 2024 and corrected it on August 1, 2024. Nothing more has been filed in this docket.

Later actions on the same rule were filed in other dockets. These are the ones I found through a Federal Register search:

- **Reconsideration (docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2024-0358):**
  - A proposal was published on 2025-01-15 (90 FR 3734) and corrected on 2025-01-17 (90 FR 5794).
  - A rule titled "Reconsideration of Standards of Performance…" was published on **2026-04-09** (91 FR 18056, doc. 2026-06808). I only saw its title and docket, not its text. I haven't confirmed what it changes.
- **Deadline extensions (docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0162):**
  - An interim final rule on 2025-07-31 (90 FR 35966).
  - A related rule on 2025-08-15 (90 FR 39333), with a technical correction on 2025-08-22 (90 FR 40975).
  - A further rule extending deadlines on 2025-12-03 (90 FR 55671).

The 2024 final rule is still the base rule, but the EPA has since extended some of its deadlines and reconsidered parts of it. To see what is currently in force, read the 2026-04-09 reconsideration rule and the 2025 extension rules. I haven't checked for litigation or other developments, so confirm those separately.

- **The original document:** 2025-12314 was published on July 2, 2025 (90 FR 28985) by the Wage and Hour Division. It proposed removing certain interpretive FLSA parts from 29 CFR Chapter V, Subchapter B, and the comment period closed August 1, 2025.
- **What happened next:** Document 2026-20523 was published on October 7, 2026 (91 FR 64129). It is titled "Statements of General Policy or Interpretation Not Directly Related to Regulations; Withdrawal of Proposed Rule." Searching the Federal Register for the same RIN returned only three documents: the proposal, a regulatory agenda entry from August 2026, and this withdrawal. There is no final rule.

The proposal is no longer pending. Since the rule was withdrawn, the interpretive parts it targeted (29 CFR parts 775, 776, 779, 782, 783, 784, 789, 793 and 794) were not removed through this rulemaking. I only saw the withdrawal's title and metadata, not its text, so I can't tell you the Department's stated reasons. You can read them at federalregister.gov under document 2026-20523.

finalAnswer:
Yes. DOE finalized the proposal, with one change to the stated rationale.

**The proposal (2025-08580):** DOE published it on May 16, 2025 (90 FR 20909) as "Energy Conservation Program: Test Procedures for Commercial Warm Air Furnaces." It proposed rescinding Appendix B, the "Thermal Efficiency Two" (TE2) test method, and keeping Appendix A, the original thermal efficiency test method. DOE said Appendix B was unduly burdensome. Comments closed in July 2025.

**The final rule (2026-20517):** DOE published it in the Federal Register on October 7, 2026. It withdraws the Appendix B test procedure, and commercial warm air furnaces stay under Appendix A. The link is https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/07/2026-20517/energy-conservation-program-test-procedures-for-commercial-warm-air-furnaces

**Rationale:** The final rule does not say Appendix B is "unduly burdensome," as the proposal did. It says Appendix B "would have an uncertain increase in representativeness that does not outweigh the likely increase in burden." It also says the withdrawal is consistent with DOE's proposed Process Rule. Under that rule, DOE would adopt the industry test procedure for certain equipment categories, including commercial warm air furnaces, except in very limited circumstances.

I haven't read the full text of the final rule, so I can't tell you its effective date or how it responds to comments. The abstract and the Federal Register listing are my only sources. I also didn't check whether any later correction or litigation affects it.

finalAnswer:
The final rule in Federal Register document 2024-00366 is effective on **May 7, 2024**.

The document is the EPA's final rule "Standards of Performance for New, Reconstructed, and Modified Sources and Emissions Guidelines for Existing Sources: Oil and Natural Gas Sector Climate Review" (89 FR 16820). It was published on March 8, 2024. The "Dates" section says: "This final rule is effective on May 7, 2024." The incorporation by reference of certain publications listed in the rule is approved by the Director of the Federal Register as of the same date.

finalAnswer:
RIN 1903-AA23 isn't an OSHA rule. It belongs to the **Department of Energy** (10 CFR Part 800, "Rescinding Regulations for Loans for Minority Business Enterprises Seeking DOE Contracts and Assistance"). OSHA's RINs start with 1218.

**The effective date is now December 24, 2026.** This comes from DOE's most recent Federal Register notice, 91 FR 54946 (Doc. 2026-17381), published August 26, 2026.

The direct final rule was first published May 16, 2025 (90 FR 20769). Its effective date has been pushed back several times:

| Delay | New effective date | Federal Register citation |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | Sept 12, 2025 | 90 FR 31137 |
| 2nd | Dec 9, 2025 | 90 FR 43539 |
| 3rd | Mar 9, 2026 | 90 FR 56967 |
| 4th | June 4, 2026 | 91 FR 10954 |
| 5th | Sept 1, 2026 | 91 FR 33069 |
| 6th (latest) | **Dec 24, 2026** | 91 FR 54946 |

DOE says it is delaying the rule again to follow Department of Justice direction under Executive Orders 14281 and 12250.

The rule has been delayed repeatedly, so another extension before December 24, 2026 is possible. I found no later notice as of today (October 8, 2026). The Federal Register's metadata field for this notice still lists "Effective Date 2025-05-16", but the notice's own text gives December 24, 2026.

If you meant an OSHA rule, send me its title or its 1218-series RIN and I'll look it up.

 Title: ●Rescinding Regulations for Loans for Minority Business Enterprises Seeking DOE Contracts and Assistance 
 
 
 
 
 Abstract: 

This action rescinds the regulations for loans for minority business enterprises seeking DOE contracts and assistance, because the regulations use race in a manner that was found to violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. In Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181, 230 (2023), the Supreme Court held that the admissions programs of two universities violated the Equal Protection Clause. The loan programs governed by 10 CFR 800 bear similar characteristics to the unconstitutional admissions programs: lacking sufficiently focused and measurable objectives justifying the use of race, employing race in a negative manner, and not containing an end point for the use of race as a criterion.

finalAnswer:
As of EPA's page, last updated October 8, 2026, the 2024 methane rule is still in force. EPA is rolling parts of it back in stages, and the broader reconsideration looks unfinished.

**Background**
- EPA published the final rule on March 8, 2024. It created the OOOOb standards for new, modified and reconstructed sources.
- The same rule created the OOOOc emissions guidelines for existing sources. States must write plans to implement the guidelines.

**Changes since then**
- **November 26, 2025:** EPA issued an interim final rule that extends several compliance deadlines for new and modified sources. It also gives states more time to submit their OOOOc plans.
- **April 2026:** EPA finalized a narrow reconsideration with two technical changes. One covers the temporary flaring provisions for associated gas. The other covers the continuous monitoring requirements for the net heating value of vent gas from flares and enclosed combustion devices, along with the alternative performance test. EPA estimates it will save industry $2.5 billion from 2024 to 2038, or about $208 million per year. EPA called it a "first step," and law-firm commentary describes the changes as limited in scope.
- **April 17, 2026:** EPA proposed amendments to the air toxics standards (NESHAP) for oil and gas production and for natural gas transmission and storage. The proposal would align them with the other rules and reduce burden. It is a separate rule from the methane standards, and I didn't find whether it has been finalized.

**What I didn't find**
- EPA's page doesn't list a final action that repeals or substantially rewrites the core OOOOb and OOOOc requirements.
- I didn't check the Federal Register, the court dockets, or the current OOOOc state-plan deadlines.

For those details, see EPA's [Oil and Gas Regulatory Timeline (PDF)](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-10/oil-and-gas-regulatory-timeline_0.pdf) and its [actions page](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-industry/actions-and-notices-about-oil-and-natural-gas).

# Actions and Notices about Oil and Natural Gas Air Pollution Standards

**Follow the links below to read about:**

*   [Oil and Gas Regulatory Timeline (pdf)](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-10/oil-and-gas-regulatory-timeline_0.pdf) (169.88 KB)
*   [New Source Performance Standards and Emission Guidelines](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-industry/actions-and-notices-about-oil-and-natural-gas#nsps)
*   [Federal Implementation Plans](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-industry/actions-and-notices-about-oil-and-natural-gas#ogfip)
*   [National Emissions Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-industry/actions-and-notices-about-oil-and-natural-gas#neshap)
*   [Control Techniques Guidelines](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-industry/actions-and-notices-about-oil-and-natural-gas#ctg)
*   [Information Requests](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-industry/actions-and-notices-about-oil-and-natural-gas#info)

## Regulatory Actions

## **New Source Performance Standards and Emissions Guidelines**

### 2026 Actions to Reduce Burden on the Oil and Natural Gas Industry

**2026 Actions to Reduce Burden on the Oil and Natural Gas Industry**

On April 4, 2026, EPA took an important first step in easing regulatory burdens and unleashing the Nation’s domestic energy supply by revising two narrow technical aspects of the Biden-Harris Administration’s Clean Air Act rules for the oil and natural gas industry. The agency is finalizing discrete technical changes to the temporary flaring provisions for associated gas in certain situations, and the requirements for continuous monitoring of the net heating value of vent gas from flares and enclosed combustion devices and alternative performance test. EPA estimates this action will save the oil and natural gas industry $2.5 billion from 2024 to 2038 (3% discount rate), equivalent to $208 million per year. 

[Read the April 2026 Final Reconsideration](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2026-final-rules-reduce-burden-oil-and).

### **2025 Interim Final Rule to Extend Compliance Deadlines**

November 26, 2025 -- EPA took an important step in unleashing the Nation’s domestic energy supply by extending several compliance deadlines in the Biden-Harris Administration’s Clean Air Act rules for the oil and natural gas industry. In this interim final rule, EPA is providing more realistic timelines for owners and operators of new and modified oil and natural gas sources across the country. In addition, the agency is giving states additional time to submit plans under the 2024 Emissions Guidelines to limit methane emissions from hundreds of thousands of existing oil and natural gas sources across the country. [Read the interim final rule](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/epas-interim-final-rule-extend-compliance).

### **2024 Final Rule to Sharply Reduce Methane and Other Harmful Pollution from Oil and Natural Gas Operations and Related Actions**

December 2, 2023 -- EPA has issued a final rule that will sharply reduce emissions of methane and other harmful air pollution from oil and natural gas operations — including, for the first time, from existing sources nationwide. The final action includes New Source Performance Standards to reduce methane and smog-forming volatile organic compounds from new, modified and reconstructed sources. It also includes Emissions Guidelines, which set procedures for states to follow as they develop plans to limit methane from existing sources. Oil and natural gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane pollution in the U.S. The final rule was published in the Federal Register on March 8, 2024.  [Read the final rule and related actions](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-industry/epas-final-rule-oil-and-natural-gas). 

### 2020 Final Policy and Technical Amendments to New Source Performance Standards for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry and Related Congressional Review Act Resolution

In August 2020, EPA announced two final rules that would make it simpler and less burdensome for the oil and natural gas industry to comply with the New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry. The two rules includes policy amendments to the 2012 and 2016 NSPS, and technical amendments to the 2012 NSPS. _On June 30, 2021, a joint Congressional resolution disapproved the 2020 final policy amendments to EPA's 2012 and 2016 New Source Performance Standards (known as the "policy rule")_. [Read the final rules and questions and answers about the Congressional Review Act Resolution to disapprove the policy rule](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2020-final-policy-and-technical-amendments).

### 2016 Final New Source Performance Standards for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry and Related Actions

May 12, 2016 - EPA announced three final rules that together will curb emissions of methane, smog-forming volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and toxic air pollutants such as benzene from new, reconstructed and modified oil and gas sources, while providing greater certainty about Clean Air Act permitting requirements for the industry. In 2018, the Agency announced amendments to two narrow provisions of the 2016 rule to address two of the “fugitive emissions” requirements in the 2016 rule that posed significant and immediate compliance concerns. [Read the 2016 final rule and the 2018 amendments](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2016-final-new-source-performance) 

### **2012 Final Air Rules for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry**

April 17, 2012 – EPA issued cost-effective regulations, required by the Clean Air Act, to reduce harmful air pollution from the oil and natural gas industry while allowing continued, responsible growth in U.S. oil and natural gas production. The final rules include the first federal air standards for natural gas wells that are hydraulically fractured, along with requirements for several other sources of pollution in the oil and gas industry that currently are not regulated at the federal level. [Read the final rules](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2012-final-rules-oil-and-natural-gas) 

## **Federal Implementation Plans for Indian Country**

### **Final Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) for Oil and Natural Gas Sources on the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation**

November 8, 2022 -- EPA signed a proposed reservation-specific Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) for oil and natural gas sources on the Indian country lands within the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation (U&O Reservation) in Utah. [Learn more the proposed FIP](https://www.epa.gov/air-quality-implementation-plans/final-fip-oil-and-natural-gas-sources-uintah-and-ouray-indian) .

### **Final Amendments to the Federal Implementation Plan for Managing Air Emissions from True Minor Sources in Indian Country in the Oil and Natural Gas Production and Natural Gas Processing Segments of the Oil and Natural Gas Sector**

March 6, 2020 - EPA has issued final amendments to streamline the Clean Air Act permitting process for certain sources engaged in oil and natural gas production activities in Indian country. The final amendments to the Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) for True Minor Sources in Indian Country in the Oil and Natural Gas Production and Natural Gas Processing Segments of the Oil and Natural Gas Sector could reduce, by up to 30 days, the time between a source owner/operator’s submission of required Endangered Species Act (ESA)/ National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) screening documents and beginning construction.

*   [Learn more about the final amendments](https://www.epa.gov/tribal-air/final-amendments-federal-implementation-plan-managing-air-emissions-true-minor-sources)
*   [Information about the 2019 proposal](https://www.epa.gov/tribal-air/proposed-amendments-federal-implementation-plan-managing-air-emissions-true-minor-sources)

### **EPA issues Final Amendments to Federal Implementation Plan for EPA’s Indian Country Minor New Source Review Program for Oil and Natural Gas Sources**

May 2, 2019 -- The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) signed amendments to the 2016 federal implementation plan (FIP) for managing air emissions from new and modified true minor oil and natural gas sources in Indian country. The FIP limits emissions of harmful air pollutants while providing streamlined construction authorization for new and modified “true minor sources” in the oil and natural gas production and natural gas processing segments of the oil and natural gas sector. The amendments would allow the FIP to continue to apply in portions of the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation that are included in an area EPA has designated as nonattainment for the 2015 national ambient air quality standards for ozone. [Learn more about the final FIP amendments](https://www.epa.gov/tribal-air/final-amendments-federal-implementation-plan-epas-indian-country-minor-new-source-review)

## National Emissions Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants

### Proposed Changes to the Air Toxic Standards for Crude Oil and Natural Gas Production Facilities and for Natural Gas Transmission and Storage Facilities

April 17, 2026 -- EPA  proposed amendments to the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) from Crude Oil and Natural Gas Production Facilities and from Natural Gas Transmission and Storage Facilities. This proposal would align the NESHAP with other Clean Air Act rules for the oil and natural gas industry while reducing the overall regulatory burden on owners and operators. [Read the proposed rule](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/air-toxic-standards-crude-oil-and-natural).

### EPA Issues Final Amendments to Remove Affirmative Defense Provisions from Two Air Toxics Standards

Oct. 16, 2024 -- EPA has issued final amendments to two air toxics standards that apply to oil and natural gas operations: the National Emissions Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) for oil and natural gas production facilities and the NESHAP for natural gas transmission and storage facilities.  The amendments remove affirmative defense provisions from the rules to make them consistent with 2014 decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. [Read the amendments and a fact sheet](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/epa-amends-two-air-toxics-standards-remove). 

#### **EPA Proposes Amendments to Two Air Toxics Standards to Remove Affirmative Defense Provisions**

Nov. 21, 2023 - EPA has proposed amendments to two air toxics standards that apply to oil and natural gas operations: the National Emissions Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) for oil and natural gas production facilities and the NESHAP for natural gas transmission and storage facilities.  The proposed amendments would remove affirmative defense provisions from the rules to make them consistent with 2014 decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. Members of the public have until December 6, 2023 to request a public hearing on the proposal. EPA will accept written comments on the proposal through January 16, 2024. [Learn more about the amendments](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/epa-proposes-amendments-two-air-toxics)

### **EPA Requests Information on Hazardous Air Pollution Emissions from Sources in Oil and Natural Gas Production, and Natural Gas Transmission and Storage**

Nov. 4, 2015 – EPA has issued a request for additional data and information on emissions of hazardous air pollutants (air toxics) that were not available in 2012 when EPA updated its major source air toxics standards for oil and natural gas production facilities, and natural gas transmission and storage facilities. The agency is requesting data on storage vessels without potential for flash emissions, and data on air toxics emissions from regulated small glycol dehydrators.

*   [Notice (PDF)](https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/FR-2015-11-27/pdf/2015-30103.pdf) - Federal Register - November 27, 2015

## **Control Techniques Guidelines**

### **EPA Issues Final Control Techniques Guidelines**

Oct. 20, 2016 - EPA has issued final Control Techniques Guidelines for reducing smog-forming volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions from existing oil and natural gas equipment and processes in certain states and areas with smog problems.

*   [Learn More](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2016-control-techniques-guidelines-oil-and)

## **Information Requests**

### **Requests for Information Under Clean Air Act Section 114**

On February 2, 2023, EPA sent requests for information under section 114 of the Clean Air Act to a number of oil and natural gas companies. [See the letters and the data](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/information-requests-under-clean-air-act)

## [Controlling Air Pollution from Oil and Natural Gas Operations](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations)

As of EPA's own pages (the actions page was last updated October 8, 2026), the 2024 methane rule is still in force. EPA has loosened parts of it and is working on a larger rollback that I didn't find as a published proposal.

**The base rule**
- EPA finalized the 2024 oil and gas methane rule in December 2023 and published it March 8, 2024.
- It is two rules, usually called OOOOb and OOOOc.
  - OOOOb sets performance standards for new, modified and reconstructed sources.
  - OOOOc sets emission guidelines for states to write plans covering existing sources.

**Changes since then**
- **November 26, 2025:** EPA issued an interim final rule extending several compliance deadlines. States also got more time to submit their OOOOc plans for existing sources.
- **April 4, 2026:** EPA finalized a narrow technical reconsideration, published in the Federal Register on April 9. It changes two things:
  - the temporary flaring provisions for associated gas in certain situations
  - the requirements for continuous monitoring of the net heating value of vent gas from flares and enclosed combustion devices, plus the alternative performance test
  - EPA estimates this saves industry $2.5 billion from 2024 to 2038, or about $208 million a year.
- **April 17, 2026:** EPA proposed amendments to the air toxics (NESHAP) standards for oil and gas production and for natural gas transmission and storage. The proposal would align them with the other oil and gas rules and reduce the burden on operators. This is a proposal, not a final rule.

**Still in progress**
- Administrator Zeldin announced a broader reconsideration of OOOOb and OOOOc on March 12, 2025.
- EPA says it is developing additional proposed amendments on a "focused scope" of issues raised by industry and other stakeholders.
- The pages I read don't show that proposal as published, so the larger rewrite is still pending.

**Caveats**
- I only read EPA's pages. I didn't check litigation or any Congressional action, and a court ruling or news report could add something I missed.
- EPA's actions page links to an "Oil and Gas Regulatory Timeline" PDF, updated this month. I didn't open it, but it's the best place to confirm the latest steps: https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/actions-and-notices-about-oil-and-0

# 2026 Final Rule to Reduce Burden on the Oil and Natural Gas Industry

## Background

On March 8, 2024, EPA [published a final rule](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/epas-final-rule-reduce-methane-and-other) expanding standards of performance for the oil and natural gas industry, commonly referred to as OOOOb and OOOOc. The 2024 Final Rule established new source performance standards (NSPS) for new, reconstructed, and modified sources and Emission Guidelines (EG) for states to develop plans for existing sources. EPA received multiple petitions for reconsideration of its 2024 NSPS and EG for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry. Many petitions focus on ways to make the current rule more workable for owners and operators. 

On May 6, 2024, [EPA notified petitioners](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/epas-final-rule-reduce-methane-and-other#:~:text=\(356.36%20KB\)-,May%206%2C%202024,-%2D%20EPA%20has%20notified) that it was granting reconsideration on two aspects of its final NSPS for oil and natural gas operations in response to petitions from industry. This reconsideration was finalized on April 4, 2026. [Read more about this reconsideration.](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2026-final-rule-reduce-burden-oil-and#O&G%20Final%20Recon%201)

On March 12, 2025, [EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced](https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/trump-epa-announces-oooo-bc-reconsideration-biden-harris-rules-strangling-american) a more comprehensive reconsideration of OOOOb and OOOOc to unleash energy dominance and continue the Nation’s trajectory as a leader in clean energy and emissions reductions. As part of this effort, EPA is developing additional proposed amendments to the 2024 Final Rule to address a focused scope of additional issues raised by industry and other stakeholders. 

## Regulatory Actions

### April 2026 Final Technical Reconsideration

April 4, 2026 - EPA took an important first step in easing regulatory burdens and unleashing the Nation’s domestic energy supply by revising two narrow technical aspects of the Biden-Harris Administration’s Clean Air Act rules for the oil and natural gas industry. The agency is finalizing discrete technical changes to the temporary flaring provisions for associated gas in certain situations, and the requirements for continuous monitoring of the net heating value of vent gas from flares and enclosed combustion devices and alternative performance test

EPA estimates this action will save the oil and natural gas industry $2.5 billion from 2024 to 2038 (3% discount rate), equivalent to $208 million per year. 

*   [Final Reconsideration for Two Technical Aspects of the 2024 Final Clean Air Act Rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/09/2026-06808/reconsideration-of-standards-of-performance-for-new-reconstructed-and-modified-sources-and-emissions)
    
*   [Fact Sheet: Final Reconsideration for Two Technical Aspects of the 2024 Final Clean Air Act Rule (pdf)](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-04/oil-and-gas-reconsideration-1_fact-sheet_0.pdf) (200.92 KB)
    
*   [Economic Impact Analysis: Final Reconsideration for Two Technical Aspects of the 2024 Final Clean Air Act Rule](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-04/2060-aw35-oil_and_gas_recon_1_eia_final.pdf)
    

### December 2024 Proposed Technical Reconsideration

December 20, 2024 - EPA proposed revisions to two narrow technical aspects of its final 2024 Clean Air Act rule to reduce methane and other harmful pollution from oil and natural gas operations. The Agency issued the proposal in response to industry petitions for reconsideration. 

*   [Proposed Reconsideration of Two Technical Aspects of the 2024 Final Clean Air Act Rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/15/2024-31227/reconsideration-of-standards-of-performance-for-new-reconstructed-and-modified-sources-and-emissions)
*   [Fact Sheet: Proposed Reconsideration of Two Technical Aspects of the 2024 Final Clean Air Act Rule (pdf)](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-03/og-proposed-reconsideration-fact-sheet.pdf) (356.36 KB, 01/15/2025)

# Frequently Asked Questions About EPA's Final Rule to Reduce Methane and Other Harmful Pollution from Oil and Natural Gas Operations

## Disclaimer

These frequently asked questions (FAQs) do not impose legally binding requirements on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, states, Tribes, or the regulated community, nor do they confer legal rights or impose legal obligations upon any member of the public. [Read the full disclaimer](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/disclaimer-frequently-asked-questions).

This page contains links to frequently asked questions about EPA's final New Source Performance Standards for new, modified and reconstructed source, and Emissions Guidelines for existing sources in the Oil and Natural Gas Sector. These rules are often referred to as "[OOOOb](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-60/subpart-OOOOb)" and "[OOOOc](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-60/subpart-OOOOc)." The rule was published in the [Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/03/08/2024-00366/standards-of-performance-for-new-reconstructed-and-modified-sources-and-emissions-guidelines-for) on March 8, 2024.  

Follow the links below to see questions and answers for a particular topic area.

*   [General Questions](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/frequently-asked-questions-general)
*   [Control Devices](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/frequently-asked-questions-control-devices)

## Regulatory Actions

## **New Source Performance Standards and Emissions Guidelines** 

### 2026 Actions to Reduce Burden on the Oil and Natural Gas Industry

**2026 Actions to Reduce Burden on the Oil and Natural Gas Industry**

On April 4, 2026, EPA took an important first step in easing regulatory burdens and unleashing the Nation’s domestic energy supply by revising two narrow technical aspects of the Biden-Harris Administration’s Clean Air Act rules for the oil and natural gas industry. The agency is finalizing discrete technical changes to the temporary flaring provisions for associated gas in certain situations, and the requirements for continuous monitoring of the net heating value of vent gas from flares and enclosed combustion devices and alternative performance test. EPA estimates this action will save the oil and natural gas industry $2.5 billion from 2024 to 2038 (3% discount rate), equivalent to $208 million per year. 

[Read the April 2026 Final Reconsideration](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2026-final-rules-reduce-burden-oil-and).

### **2025 Interim Final Rule to Extend Compliance Deadlines**

November 26, 2025 -- EPA took an important step in unleashing the Nation’s domestic energy supply by extending several compliance deadlines in the Biden-Harris Administration’s Clean Air Act rules for the oil and natural gas industry. In this interim final rule, EPA is providing more realistic timelines for owners and operators of new and modified oil and natural gas sources across the country. In addition, the agency is giving states additional time to submit plans under the 2024 Emissions Guidelines to limit methane emissions from hundreds of thousands of existing oil and natural gas sources across the country. [Read the interim final rule](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/epas-interim-final-rule-extend-compliance).

### **2024 Final Rule to Sharply Reduce Methane and Other Harmful Pollution from Oil and Natural Gas Operations and Related Actions** 

December 2, 2023 -- EPA has issued a final rule that will sharply reduce emissions of methane and other harmful air pollution from oil and natural gas operations — including, for the first time, from existing sources nationwide. The final action includes New Source Performance Standards to reduce methane and smog-forming volatile organic compounds from new, modified and reconstructed sources. It also includes Emissions Guidelines, which set procedures for states to follow as they develop plans to limit methane from existing sources. Oil and natural gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane pollution in the U.S. The final rule was published in the Federal Register on March 8, 2024.  [Read the final rule and related actions](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-industry/epas-final-rule-oil-and-natural-gas). 

### 2020 Final Policy and Technical Amendments to New Source Performance Standards for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry and Related Congressional Review Act Resolution

In August 2020, EPA announced two final rules that would make it simpler and less burdensome for the oil and natural gas industry to comply with the New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry. The two rules includes policy amendments to the 2012 and 2016 NSPS, and technical amendments to the 2012 NSPS. _On June 30, 2021, a joint Congressional resolution disapproved the 2020 final policy amendments to EPA's 2012 and 2016 New Source Performance Standards (known as the "policy rule")_. [Read the final rules and questions and answers about the Congressional Review Act Resolution to disapprove the policy rule](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2020-final-policy-and-technical-amendments).

### 2016 Final New Source Performance Standards for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry and Related Actions

May 12, 2016 - EPA announced three final rules that together will curb emissions of methane, smog-forming volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and toxic air pollutants such as benzene from new, reconstructed and modified oil and gas sources, while providing greater certainty about Clean Air Act permitting requirements for the industry. In 2018, the Agency announced amendments to two narrow provisions of the 2016 rule to address two of the “fugitive emissions” requirements in the 2016 rule that posed significant and immediate compliance concerns. [Read the 2016 final rule and the 2018 amendments](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2016-final-new-source-performance) 

### **2012 Final Air Rules for the Oil and Natural Gas Industry**

April 17, 2012 – EPA issued cost-effective regulations, required by the Clean Air Act, to reduce harmful air pollution from the oil and natural gas industry while allowing continued, responsible growth in U.S. oil and natural gas production. The final rules include the first federal air standards for natural gas wells that are hydraulically fractured, along with requirements for several other sources of pollution in the oil and gas industry that currently are not regulated at the federal level. [Read the final rules](https://www.epa.gov/controlling-air-pollution-oil-and-natural-gas-operations/2012-final-rules-oil-and-natural-gas) 

## **Federal Implementation Plans for Indian Country**

### **Final Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) for Oil and Natural Gas Sources on the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation**

November 8, 2022 -- EPA signed a proposed reservation-specific Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) for oil and natural gas sources on the Indian country lands within the Uintah and Ouray Indian Reservation (U&O Reservation) in Utah. [Learn more the proposed FIP](https://www.epa.gov/air-quality-implementation-plans/final-fip-oil-and-natural-gas-sources-uintah-and-ouray-indian) .

### **Final Amendments to the Federal Implementation Plan for Managing Air Emissions from True Minor Sources in Indian Country in the Oil and Natural Gas Production and Natural Gas Processing Segments of the Oil and Natural Gas Sector**

March 6, 2020 - EPA has issued final amendments to streamline the Clean Air Act permitting process for certain sources engaged in oil and natural gas production activities in Indian country. The final amendments to the Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) for True Minor Sources in Indian Country in the Oil and Natural Gas Production and Natural Gas Processing Segments of the Oil and Natural Gas Sector could reduce, by up to 30 days, the time between a source owner/operator’s submission of required Endangered Species Act (ESA)/ National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) screening documents and beginning construction.

Yes. The comment period was extended, and the new deadline was February 1, 2022.

- **Original period:** Document 2021-24202 is EPA's proposed rule on Oil and Natural Gas Sector Climate Review (86 FR 63110), published November 15, 2021. It set a comment deadline of **January 14, 2022**.

Yes. The effective date has been delayed six times. The latest delay moves it to **December 24, 2026**.

Document 2025-08573 is a Department of Energy direct final rule, published May 16, 2025 (90 FR 20769). It rescinds the regulations for loans to minority business enterprises seeking DOE contracts and assistance (10 CFR Part 800). It was originally set to take effect July 15, 2025, unless significant adverse comments came in.

| Delay notice | Published | New effective date |
|---|---|---|
| 2025-13127 (90 FR 31137) | Jul 14, 2025 | Sep 12, 2025 |
| 2025-17429 (90 FR 43539) | Sep 10, 2025 | Dec 9, 2025 |
| 2025-22324 (90 FR 56967) | Dec 9, 2025 | Mar 9, 2026 |
| 2026-04454 (91 FR 10954) | Mar 6, 2026 | Jun 4, 2026 |
| 2026-11057 (91 FR 33069) | Jun 3, 2026 | Sep 1, 2026 |
| **2026-17381** | **Aug 26, 2026** | **Dec 24, 2026** |

The latest notice is 2026-17381: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/26/2026-17381/rescinding-regulations-for-loans-for-minority-business-enterprises-seeking-doe-contracts-and

The Federal Register's `effective_on` field for 2026-17381 shows an odd value (2025-05-16). The notice text itself says December 24, 2026, so I used that.

I found these notices by searching on the rule's RIN (1903-AA23) and docket number (DOE-HQ-2025-0014). Both searches returned the same seven documents, and 2026-17381 is the newest. A notice published after August 26, 2026 would have shown up in that search.

The most recent official Federal Register action on RIN 1235-AA52 is a **withdrawal of a proposed rule**, published **October 7, 2026**.

- **Title:** Statements of General Policy or Interpretation Not Directly Related to Regulations; Withdrawal of Proposed Rule
- **Agency:** Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
- **Document number:** 2026-20523
- **Link:** https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/07/2026-20523/statements-of-general-policy-or-interpretation-not-directly-related-to-regulations-withdrawal-of
- **PDF:** https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-07/pdf/2026-20523.pdf

The Department is withdrawing the proposed rule it published on July 2, 2025 (90 FR 28985). That proposal would have removed parts of 29 CFR Chapter V, Subchapter B that were never issued or amended through notice-and-comment rulemaking. The withdrawal formally ends the rulemaking and removes the proposal from further consideration.

The Federal Register lists only two documents under this RIN. The other is the original proposed rule, document 2025-12314, published July 2, 2025.

finalAnswer:
The latest Federal Register document filed under docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2021-0317 is an EPA interim final rule, "Standards of Performance for New, Reconstructed, and Modified Sources and Emissions Guidelines for Existing Sources: Oil and Natural Gas Sector Climate Review: Correction." It was published August 1, 2024 as FR Doc. 2024-13206, and you can read it at https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/08/01/2024-13206/standards-of-performance-for-new-reconstructed-and-modified-sources-and-emissions-guidelines-for.

**What it did:**
- It made technical corrections to three regulations in the EPA's methane and climate rule for the oil and natural gas sector. That rule was finalized on March 8, 2024.
- The fixes covered wrong cross-references and typographical errors in the regulatory text. The EPA found these through its own review and through communications with stakeholders and the Office of the Federal Register.
- It also made small wording changes to clarify unclear language or fill omissions, so the regulatory text matched the descriptions in the final rule's preamble and other parts of the regulation.
- The EPA called the corrections minor and non-substantive. It took the action as an interim final rule and asked for comments on all aspects of it.

The docket has four earlier documents. They are the November 15, 2021 proposed rule, the December 17, 2021 comment period extension, the December 6, 2022 supplemental proposal, and the March 8, 2024 final rule.

Some later rulemakings on the same subject use different dockets. One is the reconsideration rule published April 9, 2026 (docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2024-0358). Another is the compliance-deadline extensions published July 31, 2025 and December 3, 2025 (docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0162). Those documents mention EPA-HQ-OAR-2021-0317 in their text, but they aren't filed under it.

finalAnswer:
**Is it in effect?** Yes, with caveats. The rule is 89 FR 16820, EPA's oil and gas methane rule (NSPS OOOOb and Emissions Guidelines OOOOc). It took effect on May 7, 2024, as scheduled. Many of its compliance deadlines have since been pushed back, and parts of it were revised in 2026.

**Was it delayed?** The rule's effective date was not delayed. EPA did extend several compliance deadlines inside it:

- **Jul 31, 2025, interim final rule (effective immediately):** It extended deadlines for control devices, equipment leaks, storage vessels, process controllers, and covers/closed vent systems under OOOOb. It also pushed back the start of the Super Emitter Program. And it extended the OOOOc state plan submittal deadline. A news item in my search results said states got about 10 extra months, to January 2027. I did not verify that date against the rule text.
- **Dec 3, 2025, final rule (effective Dec 3, 2025):** EPA kept the July extensions after reviewing comments. It also made further changes to the net heating value (NHV) monitoring deadline and the initial reporting deadline.
- **Aug 15, 2025:** EPA published a notice of public hearing and a comment-period extension for the interim rule. This was procedural and did not delay anything itself.

**Later substantive changes:**
- **Apr 9, 2026, reconsideration final rule (effective June 8, 2026):** This revised parts of the 2024 rule. According to an industry summary, it allows temporary flaring for up to 72 hours instead of 24. It also narrows routine NHV sampling requirements and removes the NHV monitoring exemption for associated gas. The same summary says the overall structure of OOOOb/c is unchanged. I did not read the rule itself.
- **Further revisions:** The same summary says more are still in development.
- **Aug 1, 2024 correction:** The Federal Register page also flags a correction document, 2024-13206. It is a minor correction, not a delay.

Check the current compliance dates for your specific sources against the Dec 3, 2025 and Apr 9, 2026 rules. Which dates apply depends on the type of equipment, and I did not pull the deadline tables. Also check for litigation or newer EPA actions after the Apr 2026 rule. I did not search for those.

Sources:
- [2024 rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/03/08/2024-00366/standards-of-performance-for-new-reconstructed-and-modified-sources-and-emissions-guidelines-for-existing)
- [Jul 2025 interim final rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/07/31/2025-14531/extension-of-deadlines-in-standards-of-performance-for-new-reconstructed-and-modified-sources-and)
- [Dec 2025 final rule](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/03/2025-21788/oil-and-natural-gas-sector-climate-review-extension-of-deadlines-in-standards-of-performance-for-new)
- [Apr 2026 reconsideration](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/09/2026-06808/reconsideration-of-standards-of-performance-for-new-reconstructed-and-modified-sources-and-emissions)

REQUEST INFORMATION
EPA Finalizes Revisions to OOOOb/c: What the Latest Changes Mean for Oil and Gas Operators
Apr 6
3 min read
On April 4, 2026, the U.S. EPA finalized revisions to portions of the 2024 oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act, commonly referred to as OOOOb/c. These updates follow industry petitions, additional data submitted after the 2024 rule, and a formal reconsideration process initiated in 2025. 

While the structure of the original rule remains in place, several key provisions have been adjusted to address implementation challenges, particularly around flaring and net heating value (NHV) monitoring. 

Here is what changed and what it means for your compliance program. 

What Changed in OOOOb/c 

1. Temporary Flaring Extended to 72 Hours 

The allowable duration for temporary flaring of associated gas has been extended from 24 hours to up to 72 hours for troubleshooting and repairs. 

The rule also introduces a new "exigent circumstances" provision that grants additional time beyond 72 hours in cases where site access is limited due to: 

Severe weather 

Personnel shortages 

Supply chain constraints 

Operators must document and report these events. 

2. Adjusted NHV Monitoring Requirements 
Operators are no longer required to perform routine Net Heating Value (NHV) sampling for flares or enclosed combustion devices (ECDs) unless conditions exist that could lower heating value, such as the presence of inert gases. 

3. Associated Gas Exemption Removed 
Additionally, the general exemption from NHV monitoring for associated gas at well sites has been removed. Going forward, associated gas sources will be subject to the same monitoring framework as other affected facilities. 

4. Updated Parameters for Alternative Performance Tests 
The revised rule also finalizes several updates to the alternative performance test option for both new and existing sources. Specific changes include: 

NHV grab sampling can now be conducted upstream of the inlet to the control device. 

The performance test window is set to 14 operating days, with weekend and holiday breaks allowed, provided sampling is spaced no more than 3-operating days apart from the previous sampling day. 

Block hourly averaging is required for continuous samples. 

A one-hour minimum sampling time applies to twice-daily samples, with an exception for sites where low or intermittent flow makes that duration infeasible. 

5. Sampling Demonstration Clarification 
The finalized rule also adds clarifying language confirming that the sampling demonstration can serve as an alternative to continuous monitoring for all air-assisted and steam-assisted flares and ECDs. 

What Has Not Changed 
It is important to note that the broader structure of OOOOb/c remains intact: 

Performance standards for new, modified, and reconstructed sources still apply 

States are still responsible for implementing emissions guidelines for existing sources 

Documentation, reporting, and defensibility remain central to compliance 

Current Compliance Deadlines 
The EPA issued an Interim Final Rule on December 3, 2025, extending several OOOOb compliance deadlines. Those deadlines remain in effect. 


What Oil & Gas Operators Should Do Next 

Re-evaluate NHV compliance strategies: Determine where sampling is still required and where it may no longer apply 
Review flare and ECD operations: Identify scenarios where inert gases or variable gas streams could still trigger monitoring 
Update internal procedures and documentation: Especially for flaring events exceeding 72 hours and exigent circumstances 
Monitor upcoming rulemaking: The EPA has indicated that additional revisions to the 2024 rule are still under development 

Navigating OOOOb Requirements with Alliance 
These revisions do not remove compliance obligations, but they do change how those obligations are met once they take effect.

As the June 1, 2026, NHV compliance date approaches, many facilities are operating in a narrow window where the existing requirements remain in effect, even as the EPA has finalized changes that will soon alter monitoring and testing expectations. 

Alliance Technical Group helps operators navigate this transition—clarifying what is required today, what will change once the amendments become effective, and how to implement a compliant, defensible approach that minimizes rework and enforcement risk while positioning facilities for the updated rule. 

Read the official press release on the EPA Website.

finalAnswer:
Yes. The Department of Labor withdrew the proposal with RIN 1235-AA52.

- **Withdrawal notice:** The Wage and Hour Division published it in the Federal Register on October 7, 2026 (91 FR 64129, Doc. No. 2026-20523). The withdrawal took effect October 6, 2026.
- **What was withdrawn:** The July 2, 2025 notice of proposed rulemaking (90 FR 28985), "Statements of General Policy or Interpretation Not Directly Related to Regulations" (Docket WHD-2025-0002). It would have removed the Fair Labor Standards Act interpretive and policy-statement parts of 29 CFR Chapter V, Subchapter B that were not issued or amended through notice-and-comment rulemaking. The Department would have turned them into subregulatory guidance outside the CFR.
- **Effect:** The Department says it is "formally discontinuing this rulemaking process and removing this proposal from further consideration."
- **Reason given:** Further action "no longer aligns with the Department's needs, priorities, and objectives." The notice also cites concerns commenters raised, including the effect on specific industries. Of six substantive comments, two supported the proposal and four opposed it.
- **Future action:** If the Department later decides to revise these parts, it says it will start a new rulemaking.

The notice was signed September 28, 2026, by Andrew B. Rogers, Administrator of the Wage and Hour Division. You can read it at https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2026-20523.

# AGENCY:

Wage and Hour Division, Department of Labor.

# ACTION:

Withdrawal of proposed rule.

# SUMMARY:

The Department of Labor (Department) is withdrawing its notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) published on July 2, 2025 ([90 FR 28985](https://www.federalregister.gov/citation/90-FR-28985)), which proposed to remove parts located in Title 29, Chapter V, Subchapter B of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) that were not originally issued, or subsequently amended, through notice-and-comment rulemaking. With this action, the Department is formally discontinuing this rulemaking process and removing this proposal from further consideration.

# DATES:

The proposed rule published on July 2, 2025 ([90 FR 28985](https://www.federalregister.gov/citation/90-FR-28985)) is withdrawn as of October 6, 2026.

# ADDRESSES:

The docket for this withdrawn proposed rule is available at _[https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​WHD-2025-0002](https://www.regulations.gov/docket/WHD-2025-0002)._

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Daniel Navarrete, Director, Division of Regulations, Legislation, and Interpretation, Wage and Hour Division (WHD), U.S. Department of Labor, Room S-3502, 200 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20210; telephone: (202) 693-0406 (this is not a toll-free number). Alternative formats are available upon request by calling 1-866-487-9243. If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

## I. Background

Since the 1940s, the Department's Wage and Hour Division (WHD) has provided “Statements of General Policy or Interpretations Not Directly Related to Regulations” in Title 29, Chapter V, Subchapter B of the CFR (Subchapter B), which presently spans parts 775 to 795. Most of the parts in Subchapter B provide interpretive guidance and policy statements on topics related to the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) that Congress has not specifically delegated rulemaking authority to the Department to address. While some of these parts, or provisions therein, were originally issued or subsequently amended through notice-and-comment rulemaking, many were not.

## II. Summary of the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

On July 2, 2025, the Department published an NPRM titled “Statements of General Policy or Interpretation Not Directly Related to Regulations” ([90 FR 28985](https://www.federalregister.gov/citation/90-FR-28985)), in which it proposed to remove parts located in Subchapter B that were not originally issued, or subsequently amended, through notice-and-comment rulemaking. These parts consist of interpretive rules and policy statements regarding the FLSA that do not carry the force and effect of law. The Department proposed to repurpose these parts as subregulatory guidance, remove them from the CFR, and post or provide them elsewhere.

The Department also sought comment on what provisions in Subchapter B should be retained in the CFR, and, if the rule were finalized as proposed, what kind of subregulatory guidance the Department should use to preserve interpretive rules and policy statements removed from the CFR.

The NPRM provided a 30-day comment period that ended on August 1, 2025.
